messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 75
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Sculptor
  trauma_type: Life-threatening accident
  pcl5: 75

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Meaning Seeking: I think about why the event has happened to me, Body Monitoring: constantly check body for signs of danger or injury, Avoid Physical Stress: Situations that put my body under stress
  Negative Appraisals: Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Nabil is a 75-year-old widowed sculptor who came to treatment months after a life-threatening accident in his studio, an event he still returns to in his mind with the stunned disbelief of someone who had trusted his hands and body for a lifetime. He had been moving a heavy stone form into place, working alone as he often did, when the piece shifted unexpectedly. In trying to steady it, he lost his footing and was pinned hard enough that, for a terrifying stretch of time, he could not free himself and was certain he might die there on the studio floor. What remains most vivid to him is the helplessness of feeling his body fail him at the exact moment he needed it most: the sudden weakness in his legs, the pain, the sense that the strength and steadiness he had built a life around could no longer be counted on. Since then, he has carried the conviction that something fundamental was ruined. He says, in different ways, that his body is no longer trustworthy, that what happened damaged him permanently, and that he has changed for the worse.

These beliefs have become the lens through which he now reads ordinary bodily experience. A small ache after lifting groceries, stiffness when he first stands, a flutter in his chest when he climbs stairs—Nabil treats each sensation as possible evidence that the accident left hidden injury behind. Because he has come to believe he is physically vulnerable and permanently damaged, he checks himself constantly. He presses at sore places, notices every pull in his back, takes inventory of his breathing, and scans for signs that his body is about to fail him again. He also spends long stretches thinking about why this happened to him at this stage of life, circling questions he cannot answer: whether he was foolish to keep working with stone at his age, whether the accident was some kind of punishment, whether it marked the end of the man he had been. The more certain he feels that his body has been altered beyond repair, the more he tries to protect it by avoiding anything that feels physically demanding.

That change is most visible in the studio, which had once been the center of his days and now feels charged with danger. Nabil still goes there, but he moves through it differently. He no longer attempts heavier pieces, and he avoids tasks that raise his heart rate or require straining, bracing, or prolonged standing. If he feels even a flicker of pain while positioning clay or carrying tools, he stops and studies his body until he can decide whether he is safe. He has come to believe that physical stress might expose just how damaged he really is, so he works in shorter bursts and abandons projects that would once have absorbed him for hours. He finds himself pausing in the middle of shaping a form not because he has lost the artistic idea, but because he is checking whether the tension in his shoulder means something serious. In this way, the belief that his body is unreliable pushes him toward more monitoring and more avoidance, and the studio has become less a place of mastery than a place where he watches for collapse.

Over the following months, these habits narrowed his life. He takes fewer walks, turns down invitations that would require exertion, and structures his day around conserving himself. As a widower, he had already grown used to long periods alone, but now the solitude has thickened around his routines. He spends more time sitting with his thoughts, trying to make sense of why the accident happened, and less time doing the physical work that once gave his days shape. Each bodily sensation is taken seriously, rarely dismissed. If he wakes sore, it confirms his fear that he has been permanently changed; once that thought takes hold, he becomes more vigilant about his body and more determined to avoid strain for the rest of the day. The pattern feels sensible to him, even necessary. What frightens him most is not pain itself but the possibility of discovering, too late, that his body has become fragile without warning.

He sought help only after recognizing that he was no longer simply recovering from an accident but reorganizing his entire life around the idea that his body could not be trusted. A recent afternoon in the studio unsettled him: while reaching for a tool, he felt a brief pull in his side and immediately stopped work, sat down, and spent the next hour checking himself and wondering whether he had just worsened some old damage. Looking at an unfinished sculpture, he was struck by the possibility that he might never work as he once had. By the time he came in, Nabil was not asking for pain relief so much as for some way to live without constant surveillance of his own body. He is most afraid that the accident revealed a permanent weakness and that any physical effort will confirm it. What he hopes, though he says it cautiously, is to feel at home in his body again long enough to return to his work without waiting for it to fail him.
